Chapter 4: Deploying the Reporting Service

Before you begin, confirm that the host meets the minimum requirements. The reporting service is a small daemon written in Python. It reads a single configuration file at startup, writes a log to the system journal, and exposes a health endpoint on the loopback interface. Nothing else on the machine needs to change.

The first step is to copy the archive onto the target host and unpack it under the service account's home directory. Keep the original archive in case you need to roll back to the previous release. The deployment script expects the archive name to match the release tag, so rename it if the build system produced something different.

Next, create the configuration file. Start from the sample that ships with the archive and adjust the values for your own environment. The database connection string, the listening port and the retention window are the only settings that usually change. Leave the remaining keys at their defaults unless you have a specific reason to alter them.

Once the file is in place, start the daemon and watch the journal for the first few seconds. If the service fails to start, the most common causes are a misspelled database host, a port that is already in use, or a permission problem on the log directory. Each of these is reported with a distinct exit code, so an experienced operator can tell them apart without reading the source.

The service also exposes a small HTTP interface for operators. You can pass the fields in the URL when you query a report, for example the date range and the output format, which makes it easy to bookmark a particular view. The same parameters are accepted in the body of a POST request when the field list grows too long for a query string.

To change the configuration without restarting the daemon, write the new values to disk and then load them with the reload command. Check the journal afterwards to confirm that the reload finished, because a malformed file is rejected as a whole and the old configuration stays active. If you save a copy of the previous file first, rolling back is simply a matter of renaming it and reloading again.

A note on permissions: the service account should own the configuration file and the log directory, but it should not be able to modify the binary itself. If you find yourself loosening those permissions to make a deploy work, stop and fix the ownership instead.

Finally, take a few minutes to set up monitoring. A simple check every minute against the health endpoint is enough for most deployments. Alert when the check fails three times in a row, and include the last hundred lines of the journal in the alert so that whoever is on call has something to work with. Review the alert history after the first week and remove any rule that has never fired.

When the release has been stable for a month, archive the deployment notes next to the release tag, because the next person to touch the service will be grateful for the context.
